name: Free sialic acid storage disease
aliases: infantile free sialic acid storage disease (ISSD)

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of SLC17A5, which encodes sialin, the lysosomal membrane transporter that exports free sialic acid from the lysosome
Spans a spectrum from severe infantile free sialic acid storage disease (ISSD) to the milder Salla disease common in Finland
Salla disease presents with early hypotonia, delayed development, progressive ataxia, spasticity and intellectual disability with a relatively long survival
Infantile ISSD is severe, with coarse features, hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis, nephrotic-range proteinuria and hydrops fetalis, and early death
Hypomyelination on brain MRI, including a thin corpus callosum, is a characteristic radiological clue
Diagnosis is supported by markedly increased free (unconjugated) sialic acid in urine and confirmed by SLC17A5 genetic testing
No specific therapy exists; care is supportive with developmental, neurological and, where relevant, renal support
reference.pathophysiology: Sialin is a proton-driven transporter in the lysosomal membrane that carries free sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) generated by glycoconjugate degradation out of the lysosome into the cytoplasm. When sialin is defective, free sialic acid accumulates within lysosomes across many tissues, which are consequently distended by storage. The nervous system is particularly affected, with disturbed myelination underlying the hypotonia, developmental impairment and progressive motor signs, while severe transporter loss produces the multisystem infantile phenotype with visceromegaly, bone changes and, in the most severe cases, hydrops.
additionalDifferentials: Other lysosomal storage disorders with coarse features and visceromegaly (e.g. mucopolysaccharidoses, I-cell disease)
Other causes of non-immune hydrops fetalis
Cerebral palsy or other static encephalopathies in milder presentations
additionalInvestigations: Urine free (unconjugated) sialic acid quantification (markedly elevated)
SLC17A5 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Brain MRI demonstrating hypomyelination and a thin corpus callosum
Assessment for proteinuria and renal involvement in infantile disease
Developmental and neurological evaluation to characterise the phenotype
Skin fibroblast free sialic acid measurement where available
redFlags: Non-immune hydrops fetalis or severe multisystem disease in the neonate
Feeding difficulty and respiratory compromise in the infantile form
reference.prognosis: Infantile free sialic acid storage disease is severe and usually fatal in early childhood, whereas Salla disease follows a slower course with prolonged survival and predominantly neurological disability; prognosis depends on residual sialin function.
pitfalls: Not measuring urinary free sialic acid in unexplained hypotonia with hypomyelination
Confusing free sialic acid storage disease with sialidosis, where bound sialic acid metabolism differs
Overlooking renal involvement in the infantile form
Attributing a milder phenotype to cerebral palsy without metabolic evaluation
references: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
